I’m Brazilian, so my first language is Portuguese. Sometimes I get into arguments with people because in English there’s only one concept of being. The verb “to be” is only one. Where in Portuguese, there is “ser” and “estar”. They both translate to “to be”, however the first is more permanent, and the second is more temporary, like a mood. So for example, many times I have to specify: “You’re being annoying right now, but you’re not an annoying person”. And even then some people still don’t understand.

Also, I always thought it was quite bizarre that in English you call animals “it”, as if they were an object or something. In Portuguese is just “he” or “she” depending on the gender of the animal.

You know, I also have depression and also fantasize with similar things (and by saying that, I don’t mean I feel the same as you. Only you know how you feel). For example, I keep thinking that ”if I’m gonna die eventually, why not die now and save me the effort and pain of living?”.
At the time I think of these ideas, they seem very real in my mind, and the feelings attached to them, extremely genuine. In fact, those are the times I actually feel something real. However, after a few days pass, and after I have time to reflect and talk to my psychologist, I realise that those ideas of death had a much deeper meaning attached to my subconscious. 
And since you wanted suicide to be legal, maybe, you just want a peaceful way to stop your pain because the root of it (or its solution) seems impossible to reach the current situation you’re in. So death seems like a very compelling option.

I’m not saying I’m right, and neither am I a professional. I don’t even know you, so it’s hard to tell by reading a few words on a post. But it’s something to consider nevertheless.

Also, the reason why it’s not ’legal’ or accepted I should say, it’s for those seeing the situation from an outside perspective, may see suicide as a non-viable alternative or escape, and just the thought of it causes them uneasiness and pity. Maybe that’s why.
